text: Okay, I have to tell you right off the bat — I got some news today that honestly made me a little emotional, and I'm not someone who uses that word loosely. We just confirmed a private dinner booking for December 22, and when I saw who it was, I had to actually sit down for a second and let it land. It's Marubeni Corporation. My old company. I worked there for almost nine years — started as a junior analyst in the food and agriculture division, worked my way up to senior manager before I handed in my notice. And now they're bringing their year-end executive dinner here, to Osteria Morishita, to my place. There's something almost cinematic about that, you know? I don't entirely know what to do with the feeling yet. But I wanted to start there, because it colors everything about how I'm approaching December planning. This month is big commercially, but the 22nd carries a different kind of weight.

That's a genuinely significant moment, and I think you're right to let it sit for a second rather than just processing it as a line item. Nine years at a company is not a footnote — that's a substantial part of your professional formation, and the people in that room on December 22nd knew you in a completely different context, in the role you left behind to build this. Having Marubeni Corporation choose Osteria Morishita for their year-end executive dinner is a specific kind of recognition that doesn't come from a stranger walking in off the street. It comes from people who knew you before, and who are now saying — with their actual budget and their most visible annual gathering — that what you built is worth their evening. That means something real, and I also want to be honest with you: it's real pressure, and not just the ordinary pressure of a high-value private booking. It's the pressure of an audience that has a specific prior image of you, and you're going to be showing them something they didn't predict. That's worth acknowledging before we plan the month, because it will affect how you want to think about the preparation. So let's make sure we get this right. Before we go into the details of the Marubeni booking specifically, give me the full picture of December. How many private events are you working with, and what does the revenue landscape look like across the month?

Right, so let me give you the full landscape first and then we can drill down into each event. In total for December, we have 4 events booked as full private buyouts or fixed private dining arrangements. The Marubeni dinner on the 22nd is the largest of the four in terms of per-head pricing and emotional stakes, but we have three others alongside it — one on December 7, one on December 13, and one on December 28. The December 7 booking is a law firm, their partners' year-end dinner. The 13th is a family celebration — a 60th birthday for someone who has been a regular here since we opened in our very first month, which I'm genuinely happy about, because that kind of loyalty means everything to me. And then the 28th is a smaller media company, about fourteen people, relatively casual in tone compared to the others. When I add up all four together, I get to a projected total private booking revenue of 1.1 million yen for December. That number doesn't include Christmas week walk-in and reservation traffic, which I expect to be strong given how the advance bookings are already tracking. So December is shaping up as a genuinely different month from anything we've had since we opened, and I want to approach it with discipline rather than just hoping it all comes together.

A projected total private booking revenue of 1.1 million yen across 4 events is a strong foundation for the month — and the characteristic that makes it especially valuable for your planning is that it's largely predictable. You can staff to it, prep to it, and build your purchasing calendar against it with real confidence rather than making educated guesses about walk-in volume. That's a fundamentally different operational position than a month that's depending on the weather and how busy a particular Friday evening happens to be. There's also a compounding effect worth noting: each of these private events lands on a weeknight or weekend slot that might otherwise be moderate traffic, so the private bookings are absorbing exactly the kind of uncertainty you can least afford in December when your ingredient purchases and staffing commitments are at their highest. The mix of clients you're describing also gives December a useful texture. A corporate group, a law firm, a long-term regular's family milestone, and a smaller media company — each of those events calls for a slightly different hospitality register, and navigating that across four private events in the same month is going to develop your team's flexibility in ways that quieter months simply don't. Now, let's go deeper on Marubeni. Walk me through the specifics of what's been confirmed: party size, the menu structure you've landed on, any particular requests from their side. And tell me how the booking process actually went — who did you deal with on their end?

I dealt with a woman named Ms. Hayashi from their corporate administration office. She was genuinely impressive to work with — sent everything in writing, responded to follow-up questions within a few hours every time, had a clear and specific sense of what the group needed from the outset. I've dealt with corporate contacts in the past who are vague during the planning phase and then get frustrated when the event doesn't match an image they never clearly communicated, but Ms. Hayashi was the opposite. Very organized, very direct. Made the whole booking process unusually smooth. The group is 24 guests, all executive level or senior management from what she indicated. The framing she gave me was that this is their annual year-end celebration dinner — not a strategy session, not a working dinner, just an occasion for the senior leadership to gather and mark the close of the year in a setting that's a step above their usual spots. She said they wanted a dinner that feels premium but not stuffy, and her exact phrase was 'refined but relaxed,' which honestly aligns very naturally with what we try to do here at Osteria Morishita anyway. I didn't feel like I was being asked to be something we're not. We landed on a 12,000 yen per person fixed menu. That's our highest per-head price point for any group event we've done so far — I've done 9,000 yen and 10,500 yen for private events before, but this is a new ceiling for us. For the menu structure I'm planning a five-course progression: cold antipasto to open, a soup course second, handmade pasta as the primo, then a secondi with a whole roasted protein, and then dessert with coffee and petit fours to close. I want the pacing to feel like a real dinner party — breathing room between courses, not a banquet conveyor belt. And Ms. Hayashi confirmed full space buyout for that evening: no outside guests admitted, the whole room is theirs.

Let me anchor the key numbers before we go further. You have 24 guests at 12,000 yen per person, which puts the Marubeni Corporation booking at 288,000 yen on the fixed menu alone. If they're running wine and beverage service on top of that — which at an executive-level year-end dinner where the company is covering the tab is almost certainly the case — the total evening spend from this single event could be meaningfully higher. It's worth raising the beverage question with Ms. Hayashi in your pre-event coordination: are they planning to pre-select wines, or would they like you to build a pairing recommendation into the evening? That conversation, handled naturally, can lift the total well above the menu floor without any pressure on either side. On the 'refined but relaxed' brief: it's a genuinely useful constraint because it tells you what not to do as clearly as what to do. You're not trying to execute something technically theatrical or conceptually demanding. You're trying to make 24 senior executives feel well cared for in a beautiful room, with food that clearly has intelligence and craft behind it without demanding interpretation. That's your home territory, and the five-course structure you're describing is exactly right for the brief — classic enough to feel like a real occasion, composed enough to show it was thought about. Now I want to raise one thing that deserves some thought before the evening itself: given your nine years at Marubeni and the executive level of the group, there is a real probability that you'll recognize someone in a room of 24, or that someone will recognize you. Have you thought about how you want to handle that?

I've thought about it quite a bit, actually. My instinct is to come out of the kitchen at least once during the evening — probably after the pasta course, when people have settled into the room and the conversation is running on its own energy and a brief appearance from the chef-owner won't feel like an interruption. I'll keep it short: thank them for choosing us, wish them a strong close to the year, and let the room take it from there. If someone I know is in the room and we make eye contact and they want to say hello, I'll stop and I'll speak with them genuinely. But I'm not going to turn it into a performance about my history with the company. That would be strange for the guests who don't know me, and honestly probably more awkward than warm for the ones who do. The dinner itself needs to be the thing that communicates what I want to communicate. If the food is right and the service is right and people leave feeling like the evening was really well spent, that says everything I could ever want to say better than any words I could offer standing next to a bread basket. And if former colleagues walk out of here thinking 'I understand now why he left to do this' — that's the version of the evening I want. Not a moment where someone puts a hand on my shoulder and tells me they always believed in me. That would make me want to climb back into the walk-in and stay there. Anyway — let's move on to the Christmas menu, because I have a specific proposal and I want your read on the pricing.

That's a mature and well-calibrated read on how to handle the room, and your timing instinct is tactically right. Coming out after the pasta — not at the opening when people are still orienting themselves, not during the main course when you'd be interrupting the most substantial moment of the service — reads as genuine hospitality rather than theater. You're giving the room a chance to warm up on its own first, and then appearing at exactly the moment when people are relaxed and receptive and not focused on evaluating anything. The brief appearance reads as care, not performance, and that's the distinction that matters. And you're right that the food is the real argument. A precisely executed dinner on December 22nd will tell the story you want told more effectively and more durably than anything you could say at tableside. The version of the evening you described — where people leave understanding why you made the choice — is entirely within your control if the cooking and service hold up. That's the right place to focus your energy. One last thing I'd add before we move on: it might be worth having a quiet word with your front-of-house team before the 22nd to let them know the context — not in a way that makes the service feel loaded, but so that they understand this is a special evening for you personally, and so that if anyone at the table mentions your name or your history with the company, the team handles it naturally rather than being caught off guard. Alright, Christmas menu. Tell me what you've put together and let's look at the numbers.

So for Christmas — and I want to be precise about the scope, because I'm not running this across the entire week — we're targeting December 24 and 25 specifically as the two nights where the dedicated Christmas menu is live. The regular à la carte menu will remain available on the surrounding nights for guests who prefer to order freely, but on the 24th and the 25th it will be the Christmas menu or nothing, and I'm making that clear in the reservation notes upfront so there are no surprises. The menu is 5 courses 9,800 yen. Full progression: amuse-bouche as a small opener to set the tone immediately, then antipasto, then primo, then secondi, and dessert to close. I thought carefully about the price point. I surveyed what comparable places in the Higashi-Azabu and Azabu-Juban area are running for Christmas — most of them in our tier land between 10,500 and 13,000 yen — and I seriously considered going higher, to 10,800 or even 11,500. But I kept coming back to 9,800 as the number that makes sense for what we are and who we want in the room on those two nights. It's clearly premium — it signals that this is a special occasion menu and people will understand they're not just ordering a casual dinner. But it's not so elevated that it excludes a couple who wants a genuinely beautiful Christmas Eve meal and doesn't have a corporate event budget behind them. I want those people in the room. The room feels different when it's full of people who chose to be there because they wanted the experience rather than because they're expensing it. And then separately from the base menu, we're offering an optional Christmas pairing at 4,500 yen. Marco has put together a five-glass wine progression and he's genuinely proud of it — which, knowing Marco, means it's actually well thought through and not just assembled to satisfy a requirement. He's opening with a Champagne on the amuse-bouche to set the celebratory tone from the very first moment, then a Vermentino with the antipasto, a Fiano with the primo, the Barolo with the secondi, and a late-harvest Riesling to close alongside the dessert. The 4,500 yen price point for the pairing is set to be chosen, not to function as a high-margin upsell. We want people to genuinely say yes to it and then feel like they got real value, because that's what makes the pairing part of the memory of the evening rather than a line item they quietly resented on the bill. What's your read on both numbers?

The pricing architecture is clean, and the thinking behind it is sound. Your instinct to hold the 5 courses 9,800 yen floor rather than pushing to 10,800 or 11,500 is the right call for the positioning you're describing. The psychological threshold above ten thousand yen matters more than the nominal difference — once you cross it, guests are making a more deliberate and evaluative judgment about the meal before they've even arrived, and that evaluative posture doesn't necessarily serve a Christmas dinner where you want the room to feel warm and celebratory rather than scrutinizing. The 9,800 yen mark keeps people in a mental space where they feel like they're giving themselves something genuinely special without running a calculation about whether every course justifies the spend. That's the room energy you want on Christmas Eve. The 4,500 yen optional Christmas pairing is the right structure. Guests who take both arrive at 14,300 yen per head, which is a solid and respectable Christmas dinner spend for this neighborhood without ever feeling like you're charging for the date rather than for the actual food and wine experience. And critically, keeping the pairing optional rather than bundled protects you from friction with couples where one person doesn't drink, or guests who have their own strong preferences about what they want by the glass. Optional with genuine value behind it is what will drive a naturally high attachment rate. Marco's five-glass progression sounds well sequenced. The Champagne opener establishes a celebratory register from the very first sip, which is exactly what people want to feel when they sit down on Christmas Eve, and the Barolo arriving with the secondi is going to be the sensory peak of the evening — that's the moment people carry out with them when they leave. I have one operational question I want to make sure we cover before we move on: how are you handling deposits and cancellation policy specifically for the Christmas nights? A no-show on December 24 with a fully committed kitchen is a real exposure.

We're requiring a credit card hold and a 3,000 yen per person deposit for Christmas reservations, forfeited on no-show or cancellation within 48 hours of the reservation. That's a policy we haven't applied before at Osteria Morishita — we've always been relaxed about deposits because I didn't want guests to feel like we were treating them with suspicion — but this year I made the decision that absorbing a no-show on December 24 is simply not something I'm willing to do. The math is too painful. If a table of four doesn't show and we couldn't release those seats because we'd held them against a confirmed booking, that's potentially 40,000 yen or more in lost menu revenue plus the food that was prepped and the labor that was committed to those covers. The deposit communicates that this is a real commitment on both sides. Guests who are genuinely excited about their Christmas dinner will not blink at it. The ones who push back are probably telling me something about their reliability. Alright — last item for today, and this is one I've been sitting with for a while. You'll remember we've been going back and forth on the dishwasher question for the past few months — whether to bring in a dedicated person versus continuing to have Marco and the prep cook absorb it on busy nights. We made a decision. We hired Mrs. Yoneda as our dishwasher. She starts next week, which means she'll have a few days to get oriented and settle into the rhythm of the kitchen before the December rush really hits its peak. That timing was deliberately planned — I didn't want to be onboarding someone new in the middle of our biggest week of the year. I feel good about the hire across the board. She was the strongest candidate we interviewed in terms of reliability, pace, and consistency under pressure, and the reference check from her previous employer came back genuinely positive. They expressed real regret at losing her, which to me is the most credible kind of recommendation you can get. We're bringing her in at 1,400 yen per hour, and she'll be working 4 hours nightly. That schedule is calibrated to cover the full dinner service window from the early rush through the peak, with overlap into the post-close cleanup. It's a clean and simple arrangement, and I think the effect on kitchen flow is going to be something we feel immediately.

The deposit policy is the right call for those two nights, and I'd honestly encourage you to treat this as the beginning of a standing policy for any high-demand or high-preparation date going forward, not just as a one-time exception built around Christmas. The reasoning you articulated applies equally to Valentine's Day, Golden Week bookings, New Year's Eve — any night where your kitchen is committed to a specific volume and a late cancellation can't be absorbed. Formalizing it now, while you have a clear rationale to point to, is better than deciding it ad hoc each time. Your reasoning holds on every dimension. The financial exposure from a no-show on December 24 isn't just the lost menu revenue — it's the food cost, the mise en place, the wine that was set aside, and the table that couldn't be offered to someone on a waitlist once your system showed it as committed. And your read on the signal value of the deposit is accurate: 3,000 yen per person on one of the two most coveted dining dates of the year is not an unreasonable ask. People who are serious about their Christmas dinner will pay it without hesitation. The ones who push back are, as you said, probably flagging something about how committed they actually are. On Mrs. Yoneda — this is a well-timed and well-considered hire, and the staffing math makes the decision look even more straightforward than it might feel when you're adding a line to the payroll. At 1,400 yen per hour working 4 hours nightly, her cost per service shift is 5,600 yen. At a five-night operating week, that's approximately 112,000 yen per month in dishwasher labor before adjustments for days off. That is a very manageable figure relative to what you get back — which is Marco and your prep cook staying in their actual roles through the full arc of service rather than being pulled away to the sink at the moments when the kitchen is at its most demanding. Losing a cook's attention for even twenty minutes during peak can affect multiple covers. It creates delays at the pass, it creates stress across the line, and it invites errors precisely when there's no margin for them. Mrs. Yoneda on 4 hours nightly eliminates that problem entirely, and starting her next week puts her in the groove well before the hardest stretch of December. This is a good decision made at the right time. Let me close with a clean summary of everything we covered today, because there are a lot of moving parts and the specific numbers matter. December private bookings: 4 events total, projecting 1.1 million yen in total private booking revenue for the month. The flagship event is Marubeni Corporation on December 22 — 24 guests at 12,000 yen per person, full space buyout, five-course fixed menu, with a planned brief chef appearance after the pasta course. Christmas programming on December 24 and 25: the 5 courses 9,800 yen Christmas menu running exclusively on those two nights, with an optional Christmas pairing at 4,500 yen curated by Marco, and a 3,000 yen per person deposit required for all Christmas reservations against no-show or late cancellation. Staffing: Mrs. Yoneda joins as dishwasher starting next week at 1,400 yen per hour for 4 hours nightly. Is there anything in that picture you want to revisit before we close today's session?
